The tracking period for a role last activity and Last Accessed data is for the trailing 400 days. This period can be shorter if your Region began supporting these features within the last year.

claim: Recent activity appears in the IAM console last accessed information within four hours.

claim: Service last accessed data counts every attempt to call an AWS API, not only successful ones, so an unexpected entry does not by itself mean the account was compromised.

claim: Temporary security credentials stay valid until they expire and cannot be revoked, but their permissions are evaluated on every request, so changing their access rights has the effect of revoking them.
question: Can temporary security credentials be revoked before they expire?

values.display: evaluated each time a request is made
values.spoken: permissions are checked on every request

qualifiers.scope: temporary security credentials issued by AWS STS

evidence.quote: After AWS STS issues temporary security credentials, they are valid through the expiration period and cannot be revoked. However, the permissions assigned to temporary security credentials are evaluated each time a request is made that uses the credentials, so you can achieve the effect of revoking the credentials by changing their access rights after they have been issued.

claim: Revoking active sessions of a role attaches a new inline policy that denies all actions to credentials issued before the chosen time; those credentials become invalid, while users who assume the role afterward are not affected.
question: What happens when an administrator revokes the active sessions of an IAM role?

values.display: issued before the specified time become invalid
denies all permissions to all actions

qualifiers.condition: only credentials issued before the revocation time

evidence.quote: All temporary credentials for that role issued before the specified time become invalid.
When you revoke permissions for a role using the procedure in this topic, AWS attaches a new inline policy to the role that denies all permissions to all actions.

claim: The revoke policy denies all permissions when aws:TokenIssueTime is earlier than the chosen time; that key exists only for requests signed with temporary credentials, so an IAM user's long-term credentials are not affected.
question: Which condition key does a role session revoke policy use, and does it affect long-term credentials?

values.display: does not affect requests that are signed with the long-term credentials

evidence.quote: This policy denies all permissions when the value of `aws:TokenIssueTime` is earlier than the specified date and time.

The `aws:TokenIssueTime` value is only present in the context of AWS requests that are signed with temporary security credentials, so the Deny statement in the policy does not affect requests that are signed with the long-term credentials of the IAM user.

claim: Exactly one version of a managed policy is the default version, and it is the version in effect for every user, group and role the policy is attached to; a policy with a single version uses it as the default automatically.

claim: A managed policy can have up to five versions; to change it beyond five versions with the AWS CLI or API, you first delete an existing version, while the console prompts you to delete one; inline policies have no versions.

claim: IAM is eventually consistent: a successful change to users, groups, roles or policies is stored at once but takes some time to replicate across IAM, so AWS recommends keeping IAM changes out of critical, high-availability code paths.
